blocks.text: A fine-tuning project follows a fairly consistent shape across teams and tasks, define the task, collect and prepare data, choose a base model and a fine-tuning method, run training, evaluate the result, then deploy and monitor.

This topic walks through that end to end workflow at a high level, giving a map for the rest of the course, where individual modules go deep on dataset preparation, method selection, training infrastructure, and evaluation.
1. The End to End Shape of a Fine-Tuning Project

blocks.alt: The End to End Shape of a Fine-Tuning Project
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216157-257618979.png
Every fine-tuning project moves through the same broad stages in roughly this order, though real projects loop back to earlier stages frequently as they learn more.
Skipping or rushing any one of these stages is one of the most common reasons a fine-tuning project underdelivers relative to the effort put into training itself.
2. Step One, Define the Task Precisely

blocks.alt: Step One, Define the Task Precisely
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216157-846685051.png

Before collecting a single example, write down exactly what the model should do, given exactly what kind of input, producing exactly what kind of output, and how you will know a given output is correct.

A vague goal like make the model better at support replies is not yet a fine-tuning task. A precise version, given a customer message and account tier, produce a reply in this tone with this structure, is something you can actually build a dataset and an evaluation around.
3. Step Two, Collect and Curate Data

blocks.alt: Step Two, Collect and Curate Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216157-861352357.png

This is usually the most time consuming stage of the entire workflow. Raw examples, whether pulled from historical logs, written by hand, or generated with help from another model, need cleaning, deduplication, and quality filtering before they are ready for training.

The Dataset Fundamentals and Dataset Preparation modules later in this course cover this stage in significant depth, since data quality tends to matter more than almost any other single factor in fine-tuning outcomes.

blocks.title: Data quality dominates
blocks.content: A smaller, carefully curated dataset routinely outperforms a larger, noisy one, a pattern that shows up again and again across fine-tuning projects.

blocks.text: 4. Step Three, Choose a Base Model

blocks.alt: Step Three, Choose a Base Model
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216158-875046479.png
The base model you start from sets a ceiling on what fine-tuning can realistically achieve, since fine-tuning redirects existing capability rather than creating new capability from nothing.

This choice trades off raw capability against cost, latency, and how much fine-tuning data you actually have, a smaller model fine-tuned well on a narrow task often outperforms a larger model fine-tuned poorly or on too little data.
5. Step Four, Choose a Fine-Tuning Method

blocks.alt: Step Four, Choose a Fine-Tuning Method
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216422-318980745.png

With a task and a base model chosen, the next decision is how to fine-tune, full fine-tuning if you have the hardware and want maximum flexibility, or a parameter efficient method like LoRA if hardware is limited or you want faster, cheaper iteration.
This decision is covered in depth across the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and LoRA and QLoRA modules later in this course.

blocks.text: 6. Step Five, Set Up Training and Run It

blocks.alt: Step Five, Set Up Training and Run It
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216423-97995121.png

Running training means choosing hyperparameters, a learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs, then launching the job and monitoring the loss curve as it progresses, saving checkpoints along the way so you can compare different points in training.

code.content:
# A simplified training configuration sketch
config = {
    "base_model": "chosen-pretrained-checkpoint",
    "learning_rate": 2e-5,
    "batch_size": 8,
    "epochs": 3,
    "save_checkpoint_every_n_steps": 500
}
train(config, dataset=prepared_training_data)

blocks.text: 7. Step Six, Evaluate Against a Held Out Set

Before trusting a fine-tuned model, test it against examples it never saw during training, a held out evaluation set, both with automated metrics where they apply and with human review for anything subjective like tone.
This step is what turns training a lower loss number into confidence that the model genuinely improved on the task you actually care about, the two are not automatically the same thing.
8. Step Seven, Deploy and Monitor
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448216423-7873451.png

Once a fine-tuned model passes evaluation, it moves into deployment, serving real requests, at which point monitoring becomes essential, watching for quality drift, unexpected inputs the training data did not cover, and any drop in performance over time.
Feedback gathered from production, cases where the model performed poorly, becomes the seed of the next round of data collection, closing the loop back to step two.
9. Iteration, Not a Straight Line

Real fine-tuning projects rarely move through these steps once in a straight line. Evaluation often reveals a data gap that sends the team back to step two, or a chosen base model that turns out too weak, sending them back to step three.

items: Treat the first pass through this workflow as a baseline, not a finished product
Keep evaluation examples separate from training data from the very first version of the dataset
Budget time for at least one more round of data collection after the first evaluation
Keep the task definition visible throughout, so later decisions stay anchored to the original goal

blocks.text: Worked Example

A team defines their task precisely, given a support ticket and account tier, produce a reply matching their house style within two paragraphs. They collect three thousand historical replies, clean and deduplicate them, then hold out three hundred as an evaluation set.

They choose a mid sized base model and a parameter efficient fine-tuning method given limited hardware, train for three epochs, and evaluate against the held out set, finding the model handles simple tickets well but struggles with edge cases involving refunds.

They go back to step two, collecting two hundred additional refund specific examples, retrain, and re-evaluate, this time passing their quality bar before deploying and setting up monitoring for the first month in production.
Common Mistakes

items: Starting to collect data before the task definition is precise enough to know what a correct example even looks like
Skipping a held out evaluation set and judging quality only by training loss
Treating deployment as the final step rather than the start of an ongoing feedback and monitoring loop
Choosing a fine-tuning method before confirming the available hardware can actually support it

blocks.text: Practice

Sketch out this seven step workflow for a fine-tuning idea you have in mind, writing one or two sentences per step. Notice which step you have the least clarity on, that is usually the step to focus on first.
Key Takeaway

A fine-tuning project moves through defining the task, collecting data, choosing a model and method, training, evaluating, and deploying, and treating this as an iterative loop rather than a single pass is what separates fine-tuning projects that actually ship from ones that stall after the first disappointing evaluation.
